title: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust (Act No. 20676)
authors: National Assembly of the Republic of Korea (official English translation by the Korea Law Translation Center)
institution: Government of the Republic of Korea
verification: Title page of the official KLRI English translation read at origin 2026-11-05; act number, promulgation (2025-01-21) and enforcement (2026-01-22), high-impact AI scope and institutional provisions cross-checked on CSET's translation page. Full statute text not read.
relevance: Korea's comprehensive AI statute, among the first national AI laws of a major AI economy, balancing industry promotion with risk regulation. It creates a National AI Committee as an 'AI control tower', establishes an AI safety research institute, defines 'high-impact AI' (energy, drinking water, healthcare, nuclear, biometric criminal investigation, employment and lending decisions, transport, government decision-making, student assessment) with operator obligations, and requires foreign AI companies serving Korea to designate a domestic representative. Its promotion-first, penalty-light design is the clearest East Asian counter-model to the EU AI Act. Enforcement began January 2026.

title: Projeto de Lei No. 2338/2023 - Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (approved by the Federal Senate)
authors: Senado Federal (author: Sen. Rodrigo Pacheco; rapporteur: Sen. Eduardo Gomes)

relevance: The official record of Brazil's AI bill, which the Senate approved in December 2024 after absorbing 244 amendments and related bills into a single substitutive; it establishes a risk-based framework with rights to explanation and human review and now awaits Chamber of Deputies revision. The page documents the legislative trajectory, the public consultation (roughly 35.8k votes for vs 31.5k against) and committee reports, making it the primary source for Latin America's most advanced AI regulatory effort. Useful for studying risk regulation built outside the EU template.

title: Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-related Technology (Act No. 53 of June 4, 2025)
authors: Government of Japan (official English translation, Japanese Law Translation, Ministry of Justice)
institution: Government of Japan
verification: Official English translation read at origin 2026-11-05: purpose (Art. 1), basic principles (Art. 3), responsibilities (Arts. 4-8) and chapter structure (Basic AI Plan, Art. 18; AI Strategic Headquarters, Arts. 19-28) read directly.
relevance: Japan's first national AI law, in force from June 2025: an innovation-first framework act with no penalties, declaring AI-related technology fundamental to economy and society, setting basic principles (including transparency measures against misuse, crime and copyright infringement), and creating a cabinet-level AI Strategic Headquarters chaired by the Prime Minister plus a cabinet-decided Basic AI Plan. It channels risk governance through existing sectoral frameworks rather than a new regulator, making it the clearest non-EU regulatory counter-model. The full translation of all articles was read.

title: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation
authors: AI Governance Guidelines Development Committee, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
institution: MeitY / IndiaAI Mission, Government of India
verification: Title page and executive summary (seven sutras, six pillars, action plan) read from the official PDF downloaded 2026-11-05; MeitY landing page returned HTTP 403. Full 68 pages not read.
relevance: India's whole-of-government AI governance framework, released 5 November 2025 as voluntary, principles-based guidance rather than a binding law. It adapts seven principles ('sutras') from the RBI's FREE-AI committee report - trust as the foundation, people first, fairness and equity, accountability, understandable by design, safety/resilience/sustainability, innovation over restraint - and organises recommendations across six pillars: infrastructure, capacity building, policy and regulation, risk mitigation, accountability (a graded liability system) and institutions. It proposes an AI Governance Group supported by a Technology and Policy Expert Committee and a resourced AI Safety Institute, with short/medium/long-term action items. A test case for 'techno-legal' governance in a large Global South democracy.

institution: Government of Kenya
verification: Title page and executive summary read from the official PDF downloaded from ict.go.ke 2026-11-05 (vision, three pillars, cross-cutting enablers). Full 91 pages not read.
relevance: Kenya's first national AI strategy, released March 2025, envisioning the country as Africa's leading AI hub for model innovation. The executive summary sets out three pillars - AI digital infrastructure, a sustainable data ecosystem, and AI research and innovation - supported by enablers including an 'agile and dynamic' governance framework for ethical use, data privacy and public accountability, plus talent development. It explicitly commits to data sovereignty and a cybersecurity framework, and was built through multi-stakeholder consultation. A primary source on how African governments frame AI governance as development policy.

institution: Digital Agency of Japan
verification: Official Digital Agency announcement page read at origin 2026-11-05: v2.0 decided 12 June 2026, first edition 27 May 2025, revision via the Advanced AI Utilization Advisory Board, and the document list (guideline, overview, provisional English translation, public comment results). relevance: Japan's operational rules for how national government agencies buy and use generative AI, first issued May 2025 and revised in June 2026 after advisory-board review to keep pace with technology and international policy developments. The announcement page provides the guideline, an overview, a provisional English translation and public comment records; the guideline is organised around procurement and contract checklists tied to Japan's AI Business Operator Guidelines and the AI Safety Institute's evaluation perspectives. One of the most concrete examples anywhere of AI procurement and in-house use being governed inside the state, including handling of confidential information.

title: Governing with Artificial Intelligence: The State of Play and Way Forward in Core Government Functions
authors: OECD Public Governance Directorate (project leads: Jamie Berryhill, Barbara Ubaldi, Ricardo Zapata)
institution: OECD
verification: Foreword, acknowledgements, table of contents and the opening of the executive summary read from the official 306-page PDF downloaded 2026-11-05. Full text not read.
relevance: The OECD's flagship stocktake of AI in the public sector, built on an analysis of 200 government AI use cases across 11 core functions including tax administration, public procurement, justice and service delivery. The foreword frames the core tension: government AI adoption trails the private sector, constrained by legacy systems, skills shortages and higher transparency requirements, even though AI can improve productivity, responsiveness and accountability (only 39% of people reported moderately high or greater trust in national government in 2023 OECD data). Later chapters set out enablers, guardrails and engagement mechanisms, with a dedicated public procurement section. The best international evidence base for public-sector AI readiness.

title: Transformative Public Procurement of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Giovanni Fabio Licata
institution: Laws (MDPI), vol. 14, no. 6, article 97
verification: Abstract read via the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.3390/laws14060097 on 2026-11-05; MDPI article page returned HTTP 403. Open access.
relevance: A legal-theory article arguing that public procurement of AI is not merely a purchasing technique but 'legal infrastructure' capable of restructuring state institutions around democratic values and the rule of law. Licata analyses AI's dual role - as a tool for optimising acquisition procedures and as the object of acquisition - and highlights asymmetries of expertise between public authorities and private suppliers, algorithmic legality and accountability, and complexity added by the EU AI Act. It gives scholarly grounding to treating procurement as a regulatory lever rather than back-office administration.

title: International AI Safety Report 2026
authors: Yoshua Bengio (chair) and 100+ independent experts; secretariat at the UK AI Security Institute and Mila; expert panel nominated by 30+ countries and organisations
institution: International AI Safety Report (intergovernmental research series, DSIT 2026/001)
verification: Report description, authorship, mandate and three-question structure (capabilities, risks, risk management) read at origin 2026-11-05. Full report not read.
relevance: The second edition of the intergovernmental scientific assessment on general-purpose AI, chaired by Yoshua Bengio with senior advisers including Hinton, Russell and Acemoglu, released ahead of the India AI Impact Summit with a foreword from an Indian minister. It synthesises evidence on capabilities (gold-medal-level maths, coding agents, a widening evaluation gap), risks (misuse, malfunctions, systemic risks) and risk management (evaluations, safeguards, defence-in-depth, societal resilience), while explicitly making no policy recommendations to preserve its independence. It functions as the closest analogue to an IPCC for AI and anchors several governments' oversight institutions. Its 2026 scope is narrower than the 2025 edition, which had covered bias, privacy, environment and copyright.

title: International Network of AI Safety Institutes: Joint Mission Statement
authors: AI safety institutes and government-mandated AI safety offices of Australia, Canada, the European Commission, France, Japan, Kenya, the Republic of Korea, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States
institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes
verification: Mission statement text read at origin (ISED Canada host page) 2026-11-05: signatories, Seoul Statement lineage and the four cooperation priorities.
relevance: The founding document of the international network through which national AI safety institutes - including those of Japan, Korea, Singapore and Kenya alongside Western members - agreed to cooperate after the Seoul Summit. It sets four priorities: advancing the science of AI safety risks and capabilities, developing common testing best practices including joint exercises and shared evaluation results, facilitating shared guidance, and including countries across all regions and development levels. As the institutional skeleton of global AI oversight, it is the key reference for debates on whether technical evaluation capacity can be coordinated internationally.

title: International governance of advancing artificial intelligence
authors: Nicholas Emery-Xu, Richard Jordan, Robert Trager
institution: AI & Society (Springer), advance online publication; print 2025
verification: Full abstract read via the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1007/s00146-024-02050-7 on 2026-11-05; Springer article page is bot-gated (JS challenge). Open access.
relevance: A peer-reviewed political-science analysis that builds a taxonomy of governance forms for military-capable AI - subnational governance, nationally enforced standards, a non-proliferation-plus-norms-of-use regime ('NPT+'), verification-backed restrictions, and an International Monopoly - and red-teams each form's weaknesses. The authors argue national standards struggle in race-to-the-bottom dynamics and that there is no clear historical case of major powers restricting a powerful military technology lacking a ready substitute. They conclude it is too early to choose among regimes but identify near-term policies that pay off across all scenarios. A theoretical backbone for the institution-building and oversight debate.

title: European AI Standards - Technical Standardisation and Implementation Challenges under the EU AI Act
authors: Robert Kilian, Linda Jäck, Dominik Ebel
institution: European Journal of Risk Regulation (Cambridge University Press), vol. 16, Special Issue 3, pp. 1038-1062
verification: Abstract, author list and publication details read at origin (Cambridge Core) 2026-11-05. Open access (CC-BY).
relevance: One of the first systematic peer-reviewed analyses of how firms are actually experiencing AI standardisation under the EU AI Act, drawing on interviews with 23 European AI organisations including Mistral and Helsing across mobility, finance, manufacturing, healthcare, defence and legal tech. The authors find an implementation window likely under six months against the 12+ months needed for roughly thirty technical standards, unequal participation in standards committees, double regulation and significant annual compliance costs that fall hardest on start-ups and SMEs. They argue standards are reshaping global AI competition and acting as market-entry barriers. Documents the gap between delegation-to-standards as legal design and standardisation as industrial practice.

title: Harmonised Standards for the European AI Act
authors: Josep Soler Garrido, Sarah De Nigris, Elias Bassani, Ignacio Sanchez, Tatjana Evas, Antoine-Alexandre André, Thierry Boulangé
institution: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC139430)
verification: Publication record and content summary read at origin (JRC Publications Repository) 2026-11-05: presumption of conformity, CEN-CENELEC drafting under a Commission standardisation request, expected characteristics of upcoming standards.
relevance: The Commission's own science-for-policy brief explaining what harmonised AI standards are meant to do under the AI Act: once published in the Official Journal they will grant a legal presumption of conformity to AI systems developed in accordance with them. The JRC authors describe CEN and CENELEC drafting standards on a formal request from the Commission and set out key characteristics expected of the upcoming standards, within the roughly 2-3 year transition before high-risk obligations bite. Reading it beside critical studies (Kilian et al. 2025) juxtaposes official intent with implementation reality.

title: AI Verify Testing Framework
authors: AI Verify Foundation (developed by IMDA with PDPC and industry partners)
institution: AI Verify Foundation / Infocomm Media Development Authority, Singapore
verification: Framework page read at origin 2026-11-05: 11 principles with process-check counts, MVP launch 25 May 2022, open-sourcing 7 June 2023, generative-AI-capable update 29 May 2025, and crosswalks to the NIST AI RMF, Hiroshima Code of Conduct and ISO/IEC 42001.
relevance: Singapore's governance testing framework - the first state-backed attempt to make AI claims testable - combining process checks validated by documentary evidence with technical tests across 11 principles including transparency, explainability, safety, security, robustness, fairness and human agency and oversight. The 2025 update extends it to generative AI via the Project Moonshot toolkits, and published crosswalks map it onto the NIST AI RMF, the Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct and ISO/IEC 42001. It is the leading non-Western template for audit-style verification and explicitly targets internal compliance teams and external auditors.

title: Incident reporting and investigation under the AI Act: some insights from aviation
authors: Michael Chatzipanagiotis
institution: International Journal of Law and Information Technology (Oxford University Press)
verification: Abstract read via the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1093/ijlit/eaaf019 on 2026-11-05; OUP article page returned HTTP 403. Open access.
relevance: A peer-reviewed legal analysis of the AI Act's incident-reporting and investigation regime that borrows lessons from aviation safety while accounting for differences between the two industries. The author recommends clarifying reporting duties with a common taxonomy of risk or harm and a broader personal scope, disconnecting incident reporting and investigation from liability, establishing voluntary reporting systems, guaranteeing confidentiality and reporter protection, mandating independent investigation of at least some serious incidents, and effectively disseminating safety information - all underpinned by a strong safety culture. The most concrete scholarly blueprint for fixing post-market AI incident reporting.

title: A general framework for governing marketed AI/ML medical devices
authors: Boris Babic, I. Glenn Cohen, Ariel Dora Stern, Yiwen Li, Melissa Ouellet
institution: npj Digital Medicine (Nature Portfolio), vol. 8, article 328
verification: Abstract and key framework points read at origin (nature.com via cookie-redirect) 2026-11-05. Open access.
relevance: The first systematic assessment of the FDA's postmarket surveillance of legally marketed AI/ML medical devices, analysing the MAUDE adverse-event database for roughly 950 devices approved from 2010 to 2023. The authors conclude the existing event-based system is insufficient because the most significant AI-specific risks - concept drift, covariate shift and algorithmic instability, including subgroup miscalibration - never present as individual adverse events. They propose either enriched reporting (quarterly 'deployment conditions' updates and nutrition-label style disclosures) or moving to continuous, cooperative 'system view' governance consistent with the FDA's Total Product Lifecycle approach. A model case for post-market monitoring design beyond healthcare.

title: When Less Regulation Means More Complexity: The EU AI Liability Directive Withdrawal and Its Impact on European Technological Competitiveness
authors: Luca Nannini
institution: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2025), vol. 8, issue 2
verification: Full abstract read via the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1609/aies.v8i2.36679 on 2026-11-05; AAAI OJS page unreachable (connection reset). Open access.
relevance: Peer-reviewed analysis of the European Commission's February 2025 withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive (formalised in the Official Journal in October 2025). Nannini argues that abandoning harmonised liability rules paradoxically increases regulatory complexity by fragmenting redress across 27 national regimes, disproportionately burdening European start-ups and SMEs trying to scale across the Single Market while advantaging large non-EU firms. Drawing on sectoral evidence he shows how well-designed liability frameworks can catalyse innovation through market certainty, consumer trust and safety incentives, and proposes targeted harmonisation, regulatory sandboxes and compliance-by-design toolkits.

title: After the AI Liability Directive: Civil Liability for Healthcare AI and the Limits of EU Risk Regulation
authors: Omar Tujjar, Gabriele Ientile, Francesca Toppetti
institution: European Journal of Risk Regulation (Cambridge University Press)
verification: Full abstract read via the OpenAlex record for DOI 10.1017/err.2026.10130 on 2026-11-05. Open access.
relevance: A post-withdrawal assessment of who pays when healthcare AI harms patients, comparing three deployment archetypes - a CE-marked radiology triage tool, a machine-learning deterioration score and an ambient clinical scribe - across Ireland, Italy and Germany. The authors identify five recurrent gaps even after the revised Product Liability Directive and the AI Act: evidence asymmetry, documentation integrity, multi-actor control, warning and reliance, and causation under uncertainty. Their most actionable claim is that the immediate improvements lie upstream in governance: procurement clauses on artefact retention and exportability, explicit contractual control-point allocation, and deployment-stage assessment of whether design matches the human verification expected of clinicians.

title: Governing AI for Humanity
authors: UN High-level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence
institution: United Nations
verification: Overview and publication record read at origin (UN iLibrary) 2026-11-05; the un.org PDF returned HTTP 403. Full 101-page report not read.
relevance: The final report of the UN Secretary-General's multi-stakeholder High-level Advisory Body on AI, the most globally representative blueprint for international AI governance to date. Its overview warns that ungoverned AI could concentrate benefits among a few states, companies and individuals, and stresses that governance commitments need implementation machinery, capacity development and support for SMEs; the report's proposals (including an international scientific panel on AI and a global dialogue on AI governance) fed into the Global Digital Compact process. As a UN body output it anchors the accountability conversation beyond the US-EU duopoly. Recommendation details should be cited from the full report.

title: Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. Ross Intelligence Inc., Memorandum Opinion (D. Del. No. 1:20-cv-613-SB, February 11, 2025)
authors: Judge Stephanos Bibas, sitting by designation, United States District Court for the District of Delaware
institution: US District Court for the District of Delaware
verification: Pages 1-3 of the memorandum opinion read from the official court PDF downloaded 2026-11-05 (revised 2023 opinion; partial summary judgment granted to Thomson Reuters on fair use). Full 24 pages not read.
relevance: The first US merits ruling rejecting fair use for AI training on a competitor's proprietary content: the court held that Westlaw headnotes are original enough to be copyrightable and that Ross's use of LegalEase 'Bulk Memos' built from them was non-transformative and market-harming. Judge Bibas's opinion revises his own 2023 summary-judgment ruling and grants Thomson Reuters partial summary judgment on fair use. Commentators stress it is narrow - non-generative AI trained on a competitor's headnotes - which makes it a disciplined data point rather than a template for the generative-AI training litigation wave. Affirmed in part by the Third Circuit on 30 September 2026.

title: How Generative AI Turns Copyright Upside Down
authors: Mark A. Lemley
institution: Columbia Science and Technology Law Review, vol. 25, article 2 (DOI 10.52214/stlr.v25i2.12761)
verification: Title page, abstract and introduction read from the published PDF (Stanford-hosted copy; the journal's DOI record lists the title with 'Copyright Law' and a published date of 5 June 2024) 2026-11-05. Full article not read.
relevance: The most-cited theoretical account of how generative AI strains copyright's foundations: Lemley argues that creativity will increasingly be lodged in asking the right questions rather than creating answers, so the idea-expression dichotomy and the substantial-similarity test for infringement both come under fundamental strain, and infringement doctrine may need to be rebuilt or applied in fundamentally different ways. He accepts that training foundation models is lawful while treating output-side liability as the harder problem. Reading it beside the Thomson Reuters v. Ross opinion sets early doctrine against the deeper structural critique.
